canonical_name: ABC (bribery and corruption) risk assessment blueprint — ABC controls catalogue
description: Reference catalogue `references/abc-controls.md` of the FCP blueprint `abc-risk-assessment` (skill fcp-bp-abc-risk-assessment). Sections: Introduction; Part A. General controls: subareas and requirements for effectiveness; G-ABC-01 Governance, tone at the top and organisation; G-ABC-02 Policy framework; G-ABC-03 ABC risk assessment and risk management; G-ABC-04 Awareness, training and communication; G-ABC-05 Personnel: recruitment, screening and incentives; G-ABC-06 Due diligence on business associates; G-ABC-07 Financial controls; G-ABC-08 Non-financial controls: procurement and decision processes; G-ABC-09 Gifts, hospitality, donations and sponsorship; G-ABC-10 Conflicts of interest and related parties; G-ABC-11 Raising concerns and investigations; G-ABC-12 Customer-side controls integrated with AML; G-ABC-13 Monitoring, internal audit and management review; B.1 Financial controls; B.2 Non-financial controls; B.3 Decision-process and customer-side controls (financial institutions); Part C. Tools and evidence per ISO 37001 element; Part D. Test procedures (operating effectiveness); Part E. Gap grading scale (gap analysis variant)

canonical_name: ABC (bribery and corruption) risk assessment blueprint — ABC controls catalogue — Introduction
description:
Supports step 8 of the method.

- **Part A**: general controls, i.e. the anti-bribery management system, with requirements for effectiveness.
- **Part B**: specific controls (financial, non-financial and customer-side).
- **Part C**: tools and evidence per ISO 37001 element.
- **Part D**: test procedures.
- **Part E**: grading scale for gap analyses.

**Provenance.** The structure of Part A (subareas, requirements answered Y/N/PC, an overall rating per subarea) is taken by analogy from the team's AML template for assessing general controls. The content follows ISO 37001, the UK MoJ six principles and the team's ABC material. The requirements have not yet been used in an engagement and must be validated by the team. The lists of financial and non-financial controls in Part B come from the team's ABC trainings.

canonical_name: ABC (bribery and corruption) risk assessment blueprint — ABC controls catalogue — Part A. General controls: subareas and requirements for effectiveness
description:
**Subarea rating** (wording from the team's AML template):
- **Strong**: the assessed area has a strong framework and well-functioning processes.
- **Adequate**: the area has a framework and works reasonably well, but there are shortcomings to improve.
- **Weak**: the framework is underdeveloped and/or processes are ineffective.
- **Non-existing**: the area is not covered by a framework and/or processes are not in place in practice.

**How to answer.** Answer each requirement Y / N / PC (partly covered) with a comment and justification. Requirements marked **(critical)** cap the subarea at Weak if answered N.

metadata.section: Part A. General controls: subareas and requirements for effectiveness

canonical_name: ABC (bribery and corruption) risk assessment blueprint — ABC controls catalogue — G-ABC-01 Governance, tone at the top and organisation
description:
1. **(critical)** The board or senior management has adopted an anti-bribery policy and set objectives for anti-bribery work.
2. Top management visibly communicates that bribery is not tolerated, and acts on breaches.
3. A function responsible for anti-bribery compliance is appointed. It has competence, status, authority and independence, and direct access to the board. It may be combined with the compliance function, but not with internal audit.
4. Roles and responsibilities for ABC are documented in governing documents across all three lines.
5. The function has sufficient resources and systems.
6. The board and senior management have sufficient competence to challenge ABC reporting.
7. There are clear internal reporting lines for serious ABC weaknesses.

metadata.section: G-ABC-01 Governance, tone at the top and organisation

canonical_name: ABC (bribery and corruption) risk assessment blueprint — ABC controls catalogue — G-ABC-02 Policy framework
description:
1. **(critical)** There is a policy and code of conduct that prohibit bribery in all forms, including trading in influence and facilitation payments.
2. There are instructions or routines for gifts and hospitality, sponsorship and donations, political contributions, conflicts of interest and related parties.
3. Governing documents are reviewed at least annually and reflect the current risk assessment.
4. The policy is available to all staff and is communicated to business associates that pose more than low risk.

canonical_name: ABC (bribery and corruption) risk assessment blueprint — ABC controls catalogue — G-ABC-03 ABC risk assessment and risk management
description:
1. **(critical)** A documented bribery risk assessment exists and covers all relevant processes and both perspectives (own organisation and customers or financing).
2. There are routines to update the assessment at least annually and when significant changes occur.
3. Risk evaluation criteria and risk appetite for bribery and corruption are set and linked to policy and objectives.
4. Typologies and risk factors are described in enough detail to design specific controls.
5. The assessment has been used to design or redesign controls, due diligence thresholds or training in the last 12 months.
6. The results are reported to the board and senior management at least annually.
7. Actions are documented with an owner, a deadline and status follow-up.

metadata.section: G-ABC-03 ABC risk assessment and risk management

canonical_name: ABC (bribery and corruption) risk assessment blueprint — ABC controls catalogue — G-ABC-04 Awareness, training and communication
description:
1. There is general ABC training for all relevant staff. It covers the client's own risks and routines and how to raise concerns.
2. There is targeted training for risk-exposed roles (e.g. credit, procurement, key accounts, investments), for management and for the board.
3. Training coverage is measured, and a coverage target (e.g. at least 95 %, as in the team's AML template) is met `[TO CONFIRM: target]`.
4. Training content is updated when the risk assessment changes.
5. Key business associates are informed of the ABC policy where risk is more than low.

canonical_name: ABC (bribery and corruption) risk assessment blueprint — ABC controls catalogue — G-ABC-05 Personnel: recruitment, screening and incentives
description:
1. Background checks are performed before hiring and before transfer into positions with more than low bribery risk.
2. Risk-exposed staff confirm compliance with the ABC policy periodically.
3. Bonus and incentive schemes are reviewed for conflicts with anti-bribery objectives.
4. There are disciplinary procedures for breaches, and they are applied.
5. Staff are protected against retaliation and against threats or improper contacts from external parties.

metadata.section: G-ABC-05 Personnel: recruitment, screening and incentives

canonical_name: ABC (bribery and corruption) risk assessment blueprint — ABC controls catalogue — G-ABC-06 Due diligence on business associates
description:
1. **(critical)** There is a risk-based due diligence process for suppliers, intermediaries, brokers, agents and partners before engagement and periodically.
2. Intermediaries and brokers are subject to enhanced due diligence. This covers ownership, reputation, the need for the service, the remuneration model and links to officials.
3. Contracts contain anti-bribery clauses, audit rights and termination rights.
4. Controlled entities and joint ventures implement equivalent anti-bribery controls, or commitments are obtained.
5. Due diligence results are documented, and red flags are escalated and resolved before engagement.

metadata.section: G-ABC-06 Due diligence on business associates

canonical_name: ABC (bribery and corruption) risk assessment blueprint — ABC controls catalogue — G-ABC-07 Financial controls
description:
See Part B.1 for the control list.
1. **(critical)** Segregation of duties between initiating, approving and paying.
2. Tiered approval levels for payments, with at least two signatures on payment approvals.
3. Payments to business associates require supporting documentation and evidence that the service was delivered.
4. Periodic management review of significant or unusual transactions.
5. Accounts record payments accurately and clearly (no vague "miscellaneous" or "consultancy").

canonical_name: ABC (bribery and corruption) risk assessment blueprint — ABC controls catalogue — G-ABC-08 Non-financial controls: procurement and decision processes
description:
See Part B.2.
1. **(critical)** Credit, onboarding, investment and claims decisions above defined levels require four eyes or committee approval.
2. Procurement follows a fair and transparent tender process with defined thresholds.
3. At least two persons evaluate tenders and approve the award of contracts.
4. Placing contracts is separated from approving delivery and payment.
5. High-risk transactions require approval at a higher management level.
6. Staff have practical tools: approval ladders, checklists, forms and IT workflows.

metadata.section: G-ABC-08 Non-financial controls: procurement and decision processes

canonical_name: ABC (bribery and corruption) risk assessment blueprint — ABC controls catalogue — G-ABC-09 Gifts, hospitality, donations and sponsorship
description:
1. **(critical)** There are clear thresholds and approval requirements for giving and receiving benefits, aligned with the local code of conduct (in Sweden, Näringslivskoden).
2. Benefits above the threshold are registered, both given and received.
3. The register is reviewed for patterns, such as repeated benefits to the same counterparty or benefits around tenders.
4. Sponsorships, donations and political contributions require approval and due diligence on the recipient, and are disclosed internally.

metadata.section: G-ABC-09 Gifts, hospitality, donations and sponsorship

canonical_name: ABC (bribery and corruption) risk assessment blueprint — ABC controls catalogue — G-ABC-10 Conflicts of interest and related parties
description:
1. Staff declare conflicts of interest and outside interests at hiring and periodically.
2. Staff are prevented from handling cases involving themselves or related parties (jäv), and systems enforce this where possible.
3. Related-party transactions and loans to staff or their associates are identified and approved at the right level.

metadata.section: G-ABC-10 Conflicts of interest and related parties

canonical_name: ABC (bribery and corruption) risk assessment blueprint — ABC controls catalogue — G-ABC-11 Raising concerns and investigations
description:
1. **(critical)** There is a confidential, and where possible anonymous, whistleblowing channel that meets the legal requirements of `{{jurisdiction}}`.
2. The channel is communicated to staff and relevant business associates, and staff trust it.
3. Reports are assessed and investigated by competent and independent resources, with a defined escalation to the board.
4. Investigation outcomes lead to corrective action, and lessons feed the risk assessment.

canonical_name: ABC (bribery and corruption) risk assessment blueprint — ABC controls catalogue — G-ABC-12 Customer-side controls integrated with AML
description:
1. PEP/RCA screening and EDD are in place (assessed in the AML BWRA; reference only).
2. Adverse-media screening covers corruption-related information on customers and beneficial owners.
3. Credit assessment of corporate customers in higher-risk sectors or countries considers the use of funds and the customer's own ABC controls.
4. Transaction monitoring or investigation guidance covers bribe-type payment patterns (see `abc-typologies.md`, Part C).

metadata.section: G-ABC-12 Customer-side controls integrated with AML

canonical_name: ABC (bribery and corruption) risk assessment blueprint — ABC controls catalogue — G-ABC-13 Monitoring, internal audit and management review
description:
1. ABC KPIs and KRIs are defined and reported, for example training coverage, due diligence backlog, register entries, reports received and investigations closed.
2. Internal audit covers the ABC programme on a risk basis, and findings are followed up.
3. Top management reviews the programme at least annually. The review covers changes in context, performance trends, non-conformities, audit results, incidents, the effectiveness of actions and opportunities to improve.
4. Non-conformities lead to corrective action. Several minor non-conformities in one process are treated as a major one.
5. Documented information is retained as evidence of the assessment, reviews and actions.

metadata.section: G-ABC-13 Monitoring, internal audit and management review

| C-FIN-01 | Separation of duties |

| ID | Control |

| C-NF-01 | Using only pre-approved contractors, subcontractors, suppliers and consultants whose due diligence covers corruption risk |

canonical_name: ABC (bribery and corruption) risk assessment blueprint — ABC controls catalogue — B.3 Decision-process and customer-side controls (financial institutions)
description:
| ID | Control | Typologies addressed |
|---|---|---|
| C-DEC-01 | Four-eyes or committee approval of credit decisions above a defined level; system-enforced mandates | T-ABC-01, T-ABC-02 |
| C-DEC-02 | Monitoring of approval patterns per officer and per broker (approval rates, overrides, early defaults) | T-ABC-01, T-ABC-02 |
| C-DEC-03 | Rotation or random allocation of broker-introduced applications | T-ABC-02 |
| C-DEC-04 | Independent quality assurance of KYC approvals and alert closures (first-line QA, second-line testing) | T-ABC-03 |
| C-DEC-05 | Logging and review of access to customer data; least-privilege access | T-ABC-04 |

canonical_name: ABC (bribery and corruption) risk assessment blueprint — ABC controls catalogue — Part C. Tools and evidence per ISO 37001 element
description:
From the team's ABC material. Use this to request evidence and to judge maturity.

| ISO 37001 element | Tools and evidence to look for |
|---|---|
| Context of the organisation: bribery risk assessment | A risk assessment, updated regularly and on significant change, that involves relevant functions and covers bribery and corruption risk across the organisation |
| Leadership: tone at the top, policy, code of conduct, roles; planning: actions to address risks, objectives | An anti-corruption policy (or integrity, financial crime or code-of-conduct policy) that is updated and reflects context. Defined roles. Objectives and how they are measured. |
| Support: resources, competence, communication, documentation | Evidence of regular training for general staff and key functions; evidence of communication from the top; documented information |
| Due diligence and controls; whistleblowing | Documented due diligence; whistleblowing procedure and records of concerns raised |
| Monitoring and measurement; internal audit; top management review | Internal audit records, including reporting to top management |
| Evaluation; corrective actions; continual improvement | Records of management-system reviews, adjustments of controls and input to continual improvement, at least annually |

metadata.section: Part C. Tools and evidence per ISO 37001 element

canonical_name: ABC (bribery and corruption) risk assessment blueprint — ABC controls catalogue — Part D. Test procedures (operating effectiveness)
description:
Use these when the engagement includes testing. Sample sizes are a proposal; adjust them to population size and risk. Document each test as: test ID, control, population, sample, procedure, result, exceptions, conclusion.

| Test ID | Control | Procedure |
|---|---|---|
| TP-01 | Payments to intermediaries and consultants | Sample 10–25 payments. Check contract, due diligence, approval, evidence of service, proportionality of fee, recipient account in the contracted party's name and country. |
| TP-02 | Gifts and hospitality register | Reconcile expense claims for hospitality with register entries. Check thresholds, approvals and patterns by counterparty. |
| TP-03 | Procurement | Sample contracts above threshold. Check tender evidence, two evaluators, separation of contracting and payment approval, conflict declarations. |
| TP-04 | Credit decisions | Analyse approvals by officer and by broker (approval rate, overrides, early defaults). Sample overrides for documentation and second approval. |
| TP-05 | KYC and alert handling | Sample high-risk onboardings and closed alerts per analyst. Check EDD evidence and QA. |
| TP-06 | Background checks | Sample hires into exposed roles. Check that the check was done before start. |
| TP-07 | Conflicts of interest | Compare the declarations register with HR and ownership data. Test system blocks on related-party cases. |
| TP-08 | Whistleblowing | Walk through the channel end to end. Check anonymity options, the time to acknowledge, independence of investigation and board reporting (aggregated, no names). |
| TP-09 | Training | Compare completion records against the list of risk-exposed roles. |

canonical_name: ABC (bribery and corruption) risk assessment blueprint — ABC controls catalogue — Part E. Gap grading scale (gap analysis variant)
description:
From the team's anti-corruption gap template, based on the World Bank guidelines. Use it only when the deliverable is a gap analysis. For risk assessments, use the control scale in Part A. The template answers "Gap (Yes/No)" and grades each gap:

| Grade (Swedish) | Grade (English) |
|---|---|
| Kritiska brister | Critical deficiencies |
| Omfattande brister | Extensive deficiencies |
| Betydande brister | Significant deficiencies |
| Mindre brister | Minor deficiencies |
| Inga brister | No deficiencies |

Template columns: Chapter and paragraph | Content | Gap (Yes/No) | Description of gap | Grading of gap | Comment | Reference to internal governing documents. The questions are grouped in steps: Step 1 Assess, Step 2 Plan, Step 3 Act, Step 4 Monitor, Step 5 Report to stakeholders.

canonical_name: ABC (bribery and corruption) risk assessment blueprint — ABC regulatory and professional anchors (detailed map) — Introduction
description: Supports section 4 of `SKILL.md`. Layers follow the house order: EU, then international conventions and extraterritorial law, then standards and industry guidance, then the national layer through `{{jurisdiction}}`. State "Regulatory status as of `{{date}}`" in the deliverable and check every reference against the current version. Corruption law is changing at both EU and national level.

canonical_name: ABC (bribery and corruption) risk assessment blueprint — ABC regulatory and professional anchors (detailed map) — 1. EU baseline
description:
| Instrument | Relevance to the ABC risk assessment | Note |
|---|---|---|
| Council Framework Decision 2003/568/JHA on combating corruption in the private sector | Criminal-law baseline for active and passive private-sector bribery | Will be replaced if the EU anti-corruption directive is adopted |
| EU directive on combating corruption (proposed 2023) | Harmonised offences (incl. trading in influence, abuse of functions), sanctions, prevention | Check adoption status, transposition deadline and national implementation `[VERIFY REFERENCE]` |
| Directive (EU) 2018/1673 on combating money laundering by criminal law | Corruption is a predicate offence to money laundering | Customer-side corruption risk is also AML risk |
| AML package: Regulation (EU) 2024/1624 (AMLR, applies from 10 July 2027), Directive (EU) 2024/1640 (AMLD6), Regulation (EU) 2024/1620 (AMLA) | PEP measures, business-wide risk assessment, supervision | Cross-refer to `aml-ctf-risk-assessment`; until 2027 the national AML law implementing the current directive applies |
| Directive (EU) 2019/1937 (whistleblowing) | Channels for raising concerns, protection against retaliation | National transposition in each jurisdiction |
| EBA Guidelines on internal governance (EBA/GL/2021/05) | Conflicts of interest at institutional and staff level, including loans to related parties | Applies to credit institutions and investment firms in scope |
| MiFID II (Directive 2014/65/EU); Insurance Distribution Directive (Directive (EU) 2016/97) | Conflicts of interest and inducements in investment services and insurance distribution | Inducement rules interact with gifts, hospitality and intermediary remuneration |

canonical_name: ABC (bribery and corruption) risk assessment blueprint — ABC regulatory and professional anchors (detailed map) — 1. EU baseline
description:
| Instrument | Relevance to the ABC risk assessment | Note |
|---|---|---|
| CSRD (Directive (EU) 2022/2464) and ESRS G1 Business conduct | Disclosure on prevention and detection of corruption and bribery, training, incidents | Scope and timing changed by the 2025 simplification package `[VERIFY REFERENCE]` |

canonical_name: ABC (bribery and corruption) risk assessment blueprint — ABC regulatory and professional anchors (detailed map) — 2. International conventions and extraterritorial law
description:
| Instrument | Relevance |
|---|---|
| UN Convention against Corruption (UNCAC) | Global baseline. Basis of national offences and of the EU strategy. |
| OECD Anti-Bribery Convention; OECD Recommendation for Further Combating Bribery of Foreign Public Officials and its annex on good practice for internal controls, ethics and compliance | Risk-based compliance programme expectations, including risk assessment |
| Council of Europe Criminal Law Convention on Corruption (GRECO monitoring) | National implementation reviews. Useful context for country risk. |
| UK Bribery Act 2010, section 7 (failure of commercial organisations to prevent bribery); Ministry of Justice guidance on adequate procedures (2011) | Six principles: proportionate procedures, top-level commitment, risk assessment, due diligence, communication including training, monitoring and review. Principle 3 lists external risk categories (country, sectoral, transaction, business opportunity, business partnership) and internal factors (deficient training, bonus culture rewarding excessive risk-taking, unclear rules on hospitality and promotional expenditure and political or charitable contributions, weak financial controls, no clear anti-bribery message from top management). |
| US Foreign Corrupt Practices Act (1977); US Department of Justice guidance on evaluation of corporate compliance programmes | Extraterritorial reach (issuers, USD transactions, acts in US territory). The DOJ guidance asks whether the risk assessment is current and drives resource allocation. |

**When it matters:** apply extraterritorial law when `{{client_short}}` has a UK or US nexus. Examples are a legal presence or business there, a listing, agents or intermediaries there, or trading in USD or GBP.

canonical_name: ABC (bribery and corruption) risk assessment blueprint — ABC regulatory and professional anchors (detailed map) — 3. Standards and industry guidance
description:
| Standard | Clauses or parts used in this blueprint |
|---|---|
| ISO 37001 Anti-bribery management systems (in Sweden SS-ISO 37001) | 4.1 context factors (size, structure and delegated authority; locations and sectors; nature, scale and complexity of activities; business model; controlled entities and entities exercising control; business associates; contact with public officials; legal and contractual obligations). 4.5 bribery risk assessment (identify, analyse, assess and prioritise; evaluate existing controls; set evaluation criteria; review periodically and on significant change; retain documented information that the assessment was performed and used). 7.2.2 employment process. 8.2 due diligence. 8.3 financial controls. 8.4 non-financial controls. 8.5 controlled organisations and business associates. 8.6 anti-bribery commitments. 8.7 gifts, hospitality, donations and similar benefits. 8.8 managing inadequate controls. 8.9 raising concerns. 8.10 investigating and dealing with bribery. 9.2 internal audit. 9.3 management review. |
| ISO 37301 Compliance management systems; ISO 37002 Whistleblowing management systems; ISO 31000 Risk management | Neighbouring standards for integration |
| World Bank Group Integrity Compliance Guidelines | Used in the team's anti-corruption gap template (steps Assess, Plan, Act, Monitor, Report) |
| ICC Rules on Combating Corruption | Corporate compliance programme elements |
| Wolfsberg Group: FAQs on Risk Assessments for ML, Sanctions and Bribery & Corruption (2015); Wolfsberg ABC Compliance Programme Guidance | B&C factors overlap with ML factors (jurisdiction, government-related clients) but add third parties acting for the institution, hiring practices, charitable giving, and gifts and entertainment. Inherent risk is assessed before controls, then control design and operating effectiveness, then residual risk. |

description:

**Register in Sweden.** For most financial firms there is no supervisory obligation to perform a separate ABC risk assessment, and no administrative sanction for failing to prevent bribery comparable to AML (team observation). Write "shall" only for legal requirements (criminal law, whistleblowing, AML/PEP). Use "is expected" for standards and supervisory expectations, and "we recommend" for professional judgement.

canonical_name: ABC (bribery and corruption) risk assessment blueprint — ABC risk factors by risk area — Introduction
description:
Catalogue for steps 3–7 of the method. Select the factors that apply to `{{client_short}}`, rename them in the client's terms and add client-specific factors. The IDs are the default workbook IDs.

Sources: the team's ABC trainings (financial-sector risk areas; business versus operational risk; risk context such as procurement, third parties, brokers, large accounts, approval processes and misuse of corporate assets), ISO 37001 clause 4.1, the UK MoJ guidance (principle 3), the Wolfsberg FAQ (2015) and, by analogy, the "internal risks" factor in the team's AML tool. **Analogy:** the area structure mirrors the AML risk areas.

Column guide:
- **Driver**: why the factor raises bribery or corruption risk.
- **Data points**: what to quantify, used for likelihood and exposure.
- **Typical typologies**: IDs in `abc-typologies.md`.

canonical_name: ABC (bribery and corruption) risk assessment blueprint — ABC risk factors by risk area — BUS: Business activities, products and decision processes
description:
| ID | Risk factor | Driver | Data points | Typical typologies |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| R-BUS-01 | Credit and loan approval (consumer, mortgage, corporate) | A decision with direct economic value to the applicant can be bought. Single-person mandates and pressure to approve make it worse. | Number of decisions per mandate level; share approved by one person; overrides of scoring; early-default rate by credit officer or broker | T-ABC-01, T-ABC-02 |
| R-BUS-02 | Customer onboarding, KYC approval and alert handling | A bribe or pressure to accept a customer, skip EDD, close alerts or not report ("laundering the KYC") | Manual approvals of high-risk customers; alerts closed per analyst; exceptions granted | T-ABC-03, T-ABC-15 |
| R-BUS-03 | Investment, fund selection, mandates and capital raising | Undue rewards to influence investment or selection decisions; kickbacks in securities transactions | Assets under discretionary management; external funds selected; deals in unlisted companies; inducements received | T-ABC-08 |
| R-BUS-04 | Claims handling, collections, settlements and write-offs | A bribe to approve a claim, accept a settlement or write off debt | Claims above threshold handled by one person; manual write-offs; settlement discounts | T-ABC-13 |
| R-BUS-05 | Pricing and terms exceptions | Discretion over rates, fees and limits can be exchanged for benefits | Number and value of manual price exceptions; approval level | T-ABC-01, T-ABC-12 |
| R-BUS-06 | Access to confidential information and systems | Information or system access that criminals would pay for | Staff with broad access to customer data; access reviews; data leakage incidents | T-ABC-04, T-ABC-15 |

Columns follow the team's AML typology library (category, typology, modus operandi, indicators, risk level, affected areas, sources, update date), adapted to corruption. Use the catalogue as a starting long-list in step 4. Keep only the typologies relevant to `{{client_short}}`, rewrite the modus operandi for the client's actual processes, and set the risk level in the assessment, not here.

**Provenance:**
- *Team* = scenario named in the team's ABC trainings, proposals or talks.
- *Std* = drawn from standards and guidance (ISO 37001, OECD, UK MoJ, Wolfsberg, World Bank).
- *Analogy* = adapted from the AML typology library.

Add anonymised cases from engagements under "Examples" when the team validates the catalogue.

description:
| ID | Category | Typology | Modus operandi | Indicators (red flags) | Affected processes / roles | Link to AML or fraud | Provenance |

| T-ABC-01 | Decision bribery | Bribe for credit or loan approval (incl. mortgage) | Applicant or intermediary pays a credit officer to approve a non-creditworthy application, override scoring, or omit or conceal adverse information | Approvals concentrated on one officer; overrides without documented rationale; early defaults clustered by officer; officer's lifestyle or close ties to applicants | Credit, mortgage, corporate lending | Fraud (application fraud); AML (loan used for layering) | Team |

canonical_name: ABC (bribery and corruption) risk assessment blueprint — ABC typology catalogue (corruption scenarios) — C. Red flags for transaction monitoring (customer side)
description:
Indicators that the AML function can turn into scenarios or investigation guidance. Validate them with TM owners before use.

- Payments described as commission, consultancy or success fees to persons or entities in higher-risk countries, especially round amounts.
- Payments to accounts of relatives or associates of officials (identified via PEP/RCA screening).
- Cash withdrawals or transfers shortly before or after public procurement decisions known to involve the customer.
- Payments to entities whose owners match public officials or the customer's employees.
- Charitable donations or sponsorships by corporate customers to entities linked to officials.

metadata.section: C. Red flags for transaction monitoring (customer side)

canonical_name: ABC (bribery and corruption) risk assessment blueprint — ABC typology catalogue (corruption scenarios) — D. Questions that reveal intermediary risk
description:
From the team's ABC talks. Use them in workshops and as tests.

1. Is the intermediary needed at all?
2. Is the goods or service needed, and was it delivered?
3. How is it priced, and is the price proportionate to the service?
4. Is the person who introduced the intermediary also approving its invoices?
5. Who checks that what was delivered matches the contract?
6. Is the person who introduced the intermediary also the one doing the background check?

canonical_name: ABC (bribery and corruption) risk assessment blueprint — ABC workshops, interviews and data request — Introduction
description: Supports steps 1, 2, 5 and 6 of the method. The workshop format follows the team's AML practice of workshops with the business to confirm threats, vulnerabilities and existing controls, and the team's ABC approach of an ABC risk workshop with key functions that also builds risk awareness. Durations and numbers are proposals `[TO CONFIRM with the team]`.

canonical_name: ABC (bribery and corruption) risk assessment blueprint — ABC workshops, interviews and data request — 1. Workshop plan (typical, mid-sized financial institution)
description:
| # | Workshop | Participants (roles) | Duration | Output |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | Kick-off | Compliance / ABC owner, SAE, project owner | 60–90 min | Scope, perspectives, timeline, scales, data request sent |
| 1 | Business decision processes | Heads of credit, onboarding/KYC, investments, claims/collections; AML function | ~2 h | Confirmed typologies T-ABC-01–04, 08, 12, 13; controls described |
| 2 | Third parties and procurement | Procurement, finance, legal, owners of broker/agent channels, outsourcing owner | ~2 h | Typologies T-ABC-05, 06; third-party exposure data |
| 3 | People, culture and governance | HR, management representative, compliance, internal audit (as observer) | ~1.5 h | Typologies T-ABC-07, 09–11, 14, 15; general controls G-ABC-01–05, 09–11 |
| 4 | Validation of results | Same functions; SAE consulted | ~1.5 h | Agreed ratings, actions and owners |

Small clients: combine workshops 1–3 into one session of about 3 hours.

**Working method in each workshop:**
1. Present the long-list of typologies for the area.
2. For each typology, ask "could this happen here, and how?"
3. Describe existing controls.
4. Identify vulnerabilities.
5. Collect evidence requests.

Document participants by role only.

canonical_name: ABC (bribery and corruption) risk assessment blueprint — ABC workshops, interviews and data request — 2.1 Opening questions (all workshops)
description:
- What could drive bribery or corruption risk in your area? Which decisions are worth money to someone outside?
- Where can one person decide alone?
- Have you, or colleagues, been approached with offers, pressure or threats? How would you report it, and would you?
- Who "owns" ABC in your area?

canonical_name: ABC (bribery and corruption) risk assessment blueprint — ABC workshops, interviews and data request — 2.2 Decision processes (credit, onboarding, investments, claims)
description:
- Which decisions can be overridden manually, and who reviews overrides?
- How are applications allocated to case handlers? Can an intermediary choose its handler?
- Do you monitor approval rates, overrides and early defaults per handler and per broker?
- What happens if a handler closes many alerts or approves many high-risk customers quickly?
- How are conflicts of interest (jäv) identified and blocked in the system?
- Which external parties have influence on investment or fund selection decisions? Are inducements registered?

canonical_name: ABC (bribery and corruption) risk assessment blueprint — ABC workshops, interviews and data request — 2.3 Third parties, intermediaries and procurement
description:
Questions from the team's ABC talks:
- Is the intermediary needed? Is the goods or service needed? How is it priced?
- Is the person who introduced the intermediary also approving its invoices?
- Who checks that what was delivered matches the contract?
- Is the person who introduces a party also the one doing the background check?

Further questions:
- Which suppliers were engaged without a tender in the last 12 months, and why?
- How are commission levels for brokers and agents set and reviewed?
- Do contracts contain anti-bribery clauses and audit rights? Have audit rights been used?

canonical_name: ABC (bribery and corruption) risk assessment blueprint — ABC workshops, interviews and data request — 2.4 People, culture and governance
description:
- Which roles are considered to carry more than low bribery risk, and what follows from that (screening, training, declarations)?
- How do incentive schemes reward volume versus quality and compliance?
- How are gifts, hospitality, sponsorship and donations approved and registered? Show the register.
- How often do staff interact with public officials, and who is authorised to?
- How is staff protected against threats or improper contacts from organised crime?
- What did the last management review of ABC conclude?

canonical_name: ABC (bribery and corruption) risk assessment blueprint — ABC workshops, interviews and data request — 2.5 Interviews with risk-exposed roles (sample)
description:
Short interviews (20–30 minutes) with a few people in exposed roles, for example a credit officer, a procurement officer and a key account manager:
- Walk me through a typical decision. Where are the pressure points?
- Has anyone offered you anything to influence a decision?
- Do you know where to report concerns? Do you trust the channel?

canonical_name: Fraud risk assessment blueprint — Fraud controls catalogue — Introduction
description:
Supports step 7 of the method. The file has five parts:
- **Part A**: general controls, i.e. the fraud risk management framework.
- **Part B**: specific controls per typology.
- **Part C**: detection approaches and maturity.
- **Part D**: KPIs and KRIs.
- **Part E**: test procedures.

**Provenance**

- **Part A structure**: subareas, requirements answered Y/N/PC, and an overall rating per subarea. Borrowed by analogy from the team's AML template for general controls.
- **Part A subareas**: built from the team's list of strategic issue areas within fraud risk management:
  - regular risk assessments
  - identification of significant threats and vulnerabilities
  - adequate frameworks, policies and guidelines
  - awareness raising and competence development
  - competence in internal control
  - quality assurance in the first line
  - a competent and comprehensive control environment
  - anonymous reporting with a robust case management procedure
  - tone at the top
  - recruitment

  They are completed with the team's governance and operations lists and the COSO/ACFE principles.
- **Part C**: from the team's fraud pitch.
- **Requirements**: proposals that the team needs to validate.

canonical_name: Fraud risk assessment blueprint — Fraud controls catalogue — Part A. General controls: subareas and requirements for effectiveness
description: Rate each subarea Strong, Adequate, Weak or Non-existing. A requirement marked **(critical)** that is answered N caps the subarea at Weak.

metadata.section: Part A. General controls: subareas and requirements for effectiveness

canonical_name: Fraud risk assessment blueprint — Fraud controls catalogue — G-FRD-01 Governance, tone at the top and organisation
description:
1. **(critical)** Leadership has stated its commitment and rationale for fraud prevention. There is a board-approved fraud risk appetite or loss tolerance.
2. Roles and responsibilities for fraud prevention, detection and investigation are documented across the three lines. Ownership between the fraud function, operational risk and compliance is clear.
3. Target objectives and KPIs are set for fraud management.
4. Systems and resources are sufficient: staffing, expertise and tools.
5. Management reporting on fraud is regular and highlights risks that are acted on.

metadata.section: G-FRD-01 Governance, tone at the top and organisation

canonical_name: Fraud risk assessment blueprint — Fraud controls catalogue — G-FRD-02 Policies, instructions and guidelines
description:
1. **(critical)** A fraud policy or instruction covers external fraud, internal fraud and infiltration.
2. Governing documents are updated at least annually and reflect the risk assessment.
3. Documentation requirements are defined: what to document, and who controls the documentation.

canonical_name: Fraud risk assessment blueprint — Fraud controls catalogue — G-FRD-03 Fraud risk assessment and new product approval
description:
1. **(critical)** A documented fraud risk assessment is updated at least annually and on trigger events.
2. Significant threats and vulnerabilities are identified, typology by typology, for products, channels and internal processes.
3. The new product approval process (NPAP) and change management assess fraud risk before launch.
4. The assessment has been used to calibrate the scope of controls and detection in the last 12 months.

metadata.section: G-FRD-03 Fraud risk assessment and new product approval

canonical_name: Fraud risk assessment blueprint — Fraud controls catalogue — G-FRD-04 Awareness and competence development
description:
1. There is continuous fraud awareness training for staff, including social engineering such as phishing, vishing and tailgating.
2. Targeted training is in place for fraud operations, customer service, and staff with authority to approve or change data. Competence in internal control is ensured in the first line.
3. Customer awareness measures are in place, such as warnings in channels and campaigns.
4. Awareness is tested, for example by simulated phishing or vishing, both announced and unannounced.

canonical_name: Fraud risk assessment blueprint — Fraud controls catalogue — G-FRD-05 Recruitment, screening and insider protection
description:
1. **(critical)** Background checks are done before hiring and on transfer into sensitive roles.
2. Employee activity in sensitive roles is monitored, within legal limits.
3. Mandatory leave or rotation applies in key roles where proportionate.
4. Staff can report threats or improper approaches, and are protected.

metadata.section: G-FRD-05 Recruitment, screening and insider protection

canonical_name: Fraud risk assessment blueprint — Fraud controls catalogue — G-FRD-06 Access management and IT change control
description:
1. **(critical)** Access is role-based on least privilege, with joiner, mover and leaver processes and periodic access reviews.
2. Privileged access is restricted, logged and reviewed.
3. All production changes go through change management with segregation of duties. Emergency changes are reviewed afterwards.
4. Logs are protected against alteration and monitored for anomalies.

metadata.section: G-FRD-06 Access management and IT change control

canonical_name: Fraud risk assessment blueprint — Fraud controls catalogue — G-FRD-07 Operations and control environment
description:
1. **(critical)** Delegations and four-eyes controls cover payments, changes to customer data, credit decisions and write-offs.
2. Suspense accounts and the general ledger are reconciled, and unexplained items are escalated.
3. Changes to vendor master data are verified independently, for example by call-back.
4. First-line quality assurance is in place for fraud-sensitive processes.

canonical_name: Fraud risk assessment blueprint — Fraud controls catalogue — G-FRD-08 Customer knowledge used for fraud prevention
description:
1. Identity verification at onboarding is robust against identity theft and synthetic identities.
2. Customer data and customer risk assessment are used to delay or intercept fraudulent payments, for example expected-behaviour profiles.
3. Mule indicators are used at onboarding and in ongoing due diligence, together with the AML function.

metadata.section: G-FRD-08 Customer knowledge used for fraud prevention

canonical_name: Fraud risk assessment blueprint — Fraud controls catalogue — G-FRD-09 Authentication and payment safeguards
description:
1. Strong customer authentication is applied, exemptions are monitored, and transaction risk analysis is calibrated.
2. Payee verification (name and account match) is in place where required or available.
3. Risk-based limits, delays or holds apply, for example on new payees, first-time beneficiaries and high-risk corridors.
4. Customers are warned at the point of payment for high-risk patterns.

canonical_name: Fraud risk assessment blueprint — Fraud controls catalogue — G-FRD-10 Fraud detection and monitoring
description:
1. **(critical)** Detection covers the typologies in the risk assessment, and coverage is mapped.
2. Detection runs in real time where the payment flow requires it.
3. Rules and models are documented, tested, tuned and evaluated at least every 12 months. Material models are independently validated or challenged.
4. Detection performance is measured: detection rate, alert-to-case conversion, false positives and customer friction.
5. Data is available, of sufficient quality and integrated across channels.

canonical_name: Fraud risk assessment blueprint — Fraud controls catalogue — G-FRD-11 Investigation, case management and reporting
description:
1. **(critical)** There is a case management process with clear prioritisation, a decision order and documentation.
2. Investigations focus on both process and evaluation, and their results feed detection and the risk assessment.
3. Reporting covers police reports, suspicious transaction reports when proceeds are involved, and regulatory fraud statistics.
4. Funds are recalled and recovered where possible.

metadata.section: G-FRD-11 Investigation, case management and reporting

canonical_name: Fraud risk assessment blueprint — Fraud controls catalogue — G-FRD-12 Customer compensation and complaints
description:
1. A process exists for evaluating and managing liability for customer compensation, in line with the payment-law rules of `{{jurisdiction}}`.
2. Decisions are consistent and documented, and complaints data is analysed for fraud trends.

canonical_name: Fraud risk assessment blueprint — Fraud controls catalogue — G-FRD-13 Whistleblowing with robust case management
description:
1. **(critical)** An anonymous reporting channel is in place and communicated.
2. Reports are handled with a robust case management procedure, independent investigation and escalation to the board.

metadata.section: G-FRD-13 Whistleblowing with robust case management

canonical_name: Fraud risk assessment blueprint — Fraud controls catalogue — G-FRD-14 Third parties and outsourcing
description:
1. Fraud-relevant outsourced processes are covered by contracts, oversight and audit rights.
2. Partners and brokers are monitored for fraud indicators, such as fraud rates per broker or partner.

canonical_name: Fraud risk assessment blueprint — Fraud controls catalogue — G-FRD-15 Monitoring, KPIs and performance review
description:
1. KPIs and KRIs are defined (Part D) and reported to management.
2. Internal audit and the second line review fraud management on a risk basis.
3. Management reviews the framework and its performance at least annually and decides on improvements.

metadata.section: G-FRD-15 Monitoring, KPIs and performance review

canonical_name: Fraud risk assessment blueprint — Fraud controls catalogue — Part B. Specific controls per typology (examples)
description:
Use these as a starting point for the table "Red flag | Detective/preventive controls in place | Assessment of effectiveness".

| Typology | Preventive controls | Detective controls |
|---|---|---|
| T-FRD-01 Vishing / impersonation | Delay or hold on first payment to a new payee above a limit. Payee verification. In-app warnings. Customer-set limits. Call-back for high-risk payments. | Real-time scoring of session and payment, for example login during a call, new device, new payee or atypical amount. Mule-account detection on the receiving side. |
| T-FRD-02 Account takeover | Strong authentication; cooling-off after changes to contact details; device binding | Alerts on contact-data change followed by payments; device and location anomalies |
| T-FRD-03/04 Investment and romance fraud | Warnings for payments to crypto exchanges or new foreign beneficiaries; staff scripts for intervention | Profiling of first-time large transfers abroad; repeat transfers to new beneficiaries |
| T-FRD-06/15 CEO, invoice and payee-change fraud | Independent call-back on bank-detail changes; payee verification; dual approval | Alerts on name and account mismatch; first payment to a changed account |
| T-FRD-08/09/10 Identity and application fraud | Document and identity verification; employer and income verification; broker due diligence | Monitoring of application patterns (shared employers, addresses, templates); early-default analysis per broker |
| T-FRD-12 Card fraud | 3-D Secure / SCA; card controls; activation checks | Real-time card scoring; merchant compromise detection |
| T-FRD-13 Merchant fraud | Merchant onboarding due diligence; restricted and prohibited business lists | Chargeback and refund ratio monitoring against scheme thresholds; MCC consistency checks |

canonical_name: Fraud risk assessment blueprint — Fraud controls catalogue — Part C. Detection approaches and maturity (from the team's fraud pitch)
description:
**Detection approaches.** Assess which are in use and whether they fit the typologies:

| Approach | What it does | Assessment points |
|---|---|---|
| Rule-based scenarios | Thresholds and patterns per typology | Coverage, tuning, backlog |
| Profiling based on probabilistic models | Scores each transaction against risk parameters; scores above a threshold are flagged for investigation | Balance between sensitivity (ability to identify fraud) and customer inconvenience from blocked legitimate transactions |
| Peer-group analysis | Profiles subgroups of customers by known behaviour and compares individuals with their group | Group definitions, drift |
| Markov models | Models how users move through a series of steps, e.g. in e-banking or an internal workflow, and compares each user's progress with the normal pattern | Useful for account takeover and insider workflows |
| Random forests / decision trees | Classify activity through a series of questions, which gives a more nuanced classification than a single linear rule | Explainability, validation |
| Network analysis | Links customers, accounts, devices and counterparties | Mule networks, collusion, claims rings |

**Maturity ladder.** Place the client on this ladder and state where it needs to be to counter fraud in a real-time or near-real-time payment flow:
1. **Siloed data:** no AI capability, manual data collection, outdated workflows.
2. **Limited integration:** ML models enhance rules, with some AI integration in detection engines.
3. **Entity-centric view:** predictive analytics and machine learning across the entire customer lifecycle.
4. **AI-driven suite:** AI-powered detection and investigation, with systems that complete tasks autonomously.

In the advanced stage, develop and fine-tune the models further and hold cross-functional workshops on further changes. canonical_name: Fraud risk assessment blueprint — Fraud controls catalogue — Part D. KPIs and KRIs
description:
| KPI / KRI | Definition |
|---|---|
| Gross and net fraud loss | Per product, typology and period |
| Attempted fraud and prevention rate | Prevented ÷ attempted |
| Customer-borne losses and reimbursements | Losses borne by customers; amounts reimbursed by `{{client_short}}` |
| Detection rate | Detected cases ÷ all known cases, including those reported by customers |
| Alert-to-case conversion and false-positive rate | Per rule or model |
| Customer friction | Legitimate transactions blocked or delayed; complaints |
| Time to detect / time to block | Median minutes or hours |
| Recovery rate | Recovered ÷ lost |
| Mule accounts identified and off-boarded | Per period |
| Alert and case backlog | Number and age |
| Internal fraud incidents and whistleblowing reports | Aggregated |
| Training and awareness test results | Completion; simulated-phishing click rate |
| Access review completion and exceptions | Per review cycle |

canonical_name: Fraud risk assessment blueprint — Fraud controls catalogue — Part E. Test procedures (operating effectiveness)
description:
Sample sizes are proposals; scale them to population and risk.

| Test ID | Control | Procedure |
|---|---|---|
| TP-F01 | Detection coverage | Map each relevant typology to rules or models. Back-test confirmed fraud cases from the last 12 months: were they alerted, when, and was the payment stopped? |
| TP-F02 | Payment safeguards | Walk through a new-payee high-value instant payment. Check delay, warnings, payee verification and scoring. |
| TP-F03 | Account takeover | Sample cases of contact-data changes followed by payments. Check alerts and cooling-off. |
| TP-F04 | Application fraud | Sample approved applications flagged later as fraud. Check which verification steps failed. Analyse broker-level fraud rates. |
| TP-F05 | Access and change | Sample leavers and movers for timely revocation. Sample production changes for tickets and approvals. Review privileged sessions. |
| TP-F06 | Vendor master and payables | Sample bank-detail changes for independent call-back. |
| TP-F07 | Suspense accounts | Review ageing and unexplained items. |
| TP-F08 | Case management | Sample closed cases for documentation, decision order, police and regulatory reporting, and recovery attempts. |
| TP-F09 | Customer compensation | Sample reimbursement decisions for consistency with policy and law. |
| TP-F10 | Social engineering test (optional, with client approval) | Simulated phishing, vishing or tailgating, both announced and unannounced, tailored to the organisation and legal requirements. Report only aggregated results. |

canonical_name: Fraud risk assessment blueprint — Pilot variant: focused and scalable fraud analysis in three steps
description: Reference catalogue `references/fraud-pilot.md` of the FCP blueprint `fraud-risk-assessment` (skill fcp-bp-fraud-risk-assessment). Sections: Introduction; Principles; Steps; How the assistant should run the pilot

canonical_name: Fraud risk assessment blueprint — Pilot variant: focused and scalable fraud analysis in three steps — Introduction
description: This variant is the team's own approach, taken from its fraud pitch. It has not yet been documented as a delivered engagement, so the team needs to validate the phases, outputs and duration. Use it when the client wants a quick, data-driven answer before committing to a full fraud risk assessment or a fraud programme. Its output feeds the full assessment: typologies, data, case candidates and a first view of controls.

canonical_name: Fraud risk assessment blueprint — Pilot variant: focused and scalable fraud analysis in three steps — Principles
description:
- **Focused effort:** a rapid analysis of one selected area, or a combination of areas, such as instant payments for private customers, consumer credit applications or claims.
- **Way of working:** data-driven analysis combined with dialogue with the business, carried out iteratively with regular check-ins with the client.
- **Output:** a concrete decision basis. Should this be scaled up? How should the future way of working look?

canonical_name: Fraud risk assessment blueprint — Pilot variant: focused and scalable fraud analysis in three steps — Steps
description:
| Step | Focus | Main deliverables |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Current-state analysis (nulägesanalys) | Rapid analysis of the selected area. Identify deviating behaviours and risk indicators and concrete "case candidates". Quantify the potential: how big is the problem, and where should the client prioritise? Assess exposure from products and services, the scope and coverage of the existing fraud management framework, how fraud is handled in the organisation's structure and strategy, and the ability to identify internal fraud and infiltration. | Current-state report with quantified exposure, a list of case candidates handed to the client's investigators under the client's procedures, and the risk indicators found |
| 2. Model for controls (modell för kontroller) | Calibrate the scope of controls to prevent and detect fraud, based on the risk mapping and risk assessment. Set criteria for individual processes and for model validation. Automate detection and reporting. Design the investigation process. | Control model: proposed preventive and detective controls, detection rules or model approach, validation criteria, investigation process |
| 3. Scale up (skala upp) | Mobilise the implementation programme based on the conclusions from steps 1 and 2. | Implementation plan, business case and governance for the programme |

canonical_name: Fraud risk assessment blueprint — Pilot variant: focused and scalable fraud analysis in three steps — How the assistant should run the pilot
description:
1. Agree the area and the data access, including legal approval for personal data, before starting.
2. Use `fraud-typologies.md` to choose hypotheses to test in the data, for example inflow and outflow velocity for mules, new payee plus high amount for vishing, or broker-level early defaults for application fraud.
3. Report case candidates only to the client's authorised investigators. Never name individuals in the report.
4. Express the potential as a range, with assumptions stated, and never as a precise forecast.
5. End with the decision basis: whether to scale up, what to change, the cost and effect of the change, and the next steps.

canonical_name: Fraud risk assessment blueprint — Fraud regulatory and professional anchors (detailed map) — Introduction
description:
This file supports section 4 of `SKILL.md`. The layers follow the house order: EU, national law, national supervisory regulation, European guidelines, national guidance, then industry standards.

State "Regulatory status as of `{{date}}`" in the deliverable. Payment-fraud rules are changing fast, so check every reference against the current version, especially PSD3/PSR and the dates for verification of payee.

canonical_name: Fraud risk assessment blueprint — Fraud regulatory and professional anchors (detailed map) — 1. EU baseline
description:
| Instrument | Relevance to the fraud risk assessment | Note |
|---|---|---|
| PSD2: Directive (EU) 2015/2366 | Management of operational and security risks, including an assessment reported to the competent authority. Incident reporting. Liability for unauthorised transactions. Statistical data on fraud reported to the competent authority. | Article-level references `[VERIFY REFERENCE]`. Parts of incident reporting moved to DORA for many entities. |
| RTS on strong customer authentication and secure communication: Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2018/389 | SCA, exemptions (incl. transaction risk analysis with fraud-rate thresholds), and a requirement for transaction monitoring mechanisms to detect unauthorised or fraudulent payment transactions | |
| EBA Guidelines on fraud reporting under PSD2 | Content and frequency of payment fraud statistics | `[VERIFY REFERENCE]`: confirm the current guideline number and any amendments |
| Regulation (EU) 2024/886 (Instant Payments Regulation) | Verification of payee for credit transfers; instant payments availability | Phased dates for euro-area and non-euro Member States `[VERIFY REFERENCE]` |
| PSD3 and Payment Services Regulation (proposals 2023) | Fraud data sharing between PSPs, extended IBAN/name check, refund rights in certain impersonation fraud cases, duties for other ecosystem actors | Check adoption status and application dates `[VERIFY REFERENCE]` |
| DORA: Regulation (EU) 2022/2554 | ICT risk management, ICT incident reporting, third-party ICT risk. Relevant to cyber-enabled and internal IT fraud. | Applies from 17 January 2025 |
| Directive (EU) 2019/713 on combating fraud and counterfeiting of non-cash means of payment | Criminal-law baseline for payment fraud | |

canonical_name: Fraud risk assessment blueprint — Fraud regulatory and professional anchors (detailed map) — 1. EU baseline
description:
| Instrument | Relevance to the fraud risk assessment | Note |
|---|---|---|
| Directive (EU) 2017/1371 (PIF Directive) | Criminal law on fraud against the EU's financial interests, including serious cross-border VAT fraud | Background for VAT carousel typology |
| Directive (EU) 2018/1673; AML package (Regulation (EU) 2024/1624 from 10 July 2027; AMLA) | Fraud as predicate offence; mules and proceeds in the BWRA | Cross-refer `aml-ctf-risk-assessment` |
| Directive (EU) 2019/1937 (whistleblowing) | Anonymous reporting, protection | |

canonical_name: Fraud risk assessment blueprint — Fraud regulatory and professional anchors (detailed map) — 2. Professional frameworks and extraterritorial law
description:
| Framework | Use in this blueprint |
|---|---|
| COSO/ACFE Fraud Risk Management Guide | Five principles: fraud risk governance; fraud risk assessment; preventive and detective fraud control activities; investigation and corrective action; monitoring. They map to the general-control subareas. |
| COSO Internal Control – Integrated Framework (2013), principle 8 | The organisation considers the potential for fraud in assessing risks |
| ACFE occupational fraud classification and periodic global studies | Internal fraud taxonomy (asset misappropriation, corruption, financial statement fraud). Use the studies for benchmarks, citing the edition. |
| Fraud triangle (pressure, opportunity, rationalisation) | Internal fraud vulnerability analysis |
| Basel operational risk event types | "Internal fraud" and "external fraud" as level-1 event types. Align categories for loss reconciliation. |
| UK Economic Crime and Corporate Transparency Act 2023, failure to prevent fraud (in force from September 2025), with government guidance on reasonable procedures | Relevant for groups with a UK nexus. The guidance expects a documented fraud risk assessment. |
| ISO 31000 risk management | General risk vocabulary |

canonical_name: Fraud risk assessment blueprint — Fraud risk factors by risk area — Introduction
description:
This catalogue supports steps 2–6 of the method. Pick the factors that apply to `{{client_short}}`, rename them in the client's terms, and add client-specific factors. Tag each factor with one or more fraud categories (EXT-C, EXT-I, INT, PRC).

**Sources:**
- The team's fraud pitch: product lines (mortgages, credit cards, payment services, retail and corporate accounts, funds and securities, operational risk such as procurement), the internal-risk layer, and contextual exposure.
- Fraud types in the team's AML typology library.
- The team's AML tool, by analogy (product and customer factors, "internal risks").
- General best practice.

**Analogy:** the area structure mirrors the AML risk areas.

canonical_name: Fraud risk assessment blueprint — Fraud risk factors by risk area — Other qualitative factors (all areas)
description:
The team's triggers apply across all areas:
- New or changed activities, products or services.
- Changes to the structure or strategy of the organisation.
- External changes: market conditions, liabilities (e.g. new reimbursement rules), customer relationships.

Also consider:
- Migrations of payment or core systems.
- New detection systems or models.
- Spikes in fraud trends reported by authorities.

canonical_name: Fraud risk assessment blueprint — Fraud typology catalogue — Introduction
description:
The columns follow the team's AML typology library (category, typology, modus operandi, indicators, affected areas, sources, update date). Use the catalogue as a long-list in step 3. Keep only what is relevant, rewrite the modus operandi for the client's products, and rate the risk in the assessment, not here.

**Fraud categories:**
- **EXT-C**: external fraud against customers.
- **EXT-I**: external fraud against the institution.
- **INT**: internal fraud and infiltration.
- **PRC**: fraud proceeds through the institution.

**Provenance:**
- **Team**: the team's fraud pitch or training.
- **Lib**: fraud types (förbrott) in the team's AML typology library, which build on Swedish police and financial intelligence reports.
- **Std**: general best practice (ACFE, EU payment-fraud reporting categories).

The funds leave quickly to mule accounts. | New payee and high-value payment shortly after login; login from new device during an ongoing call; elderly customer; e-ID signing at unusual time; several payments in quick succession | Instant payments, internet and mobile bank, e-ID | PRC (mules); liability rules | Team, Lib |

canonical_name: Fraud risk assessment blueprint — Fraud typology catalogue — Takeaways from the team's VAT-fraud training
description:
The team's training notes these points, which are useful for corporate-banking and factoring clients:

- VAT fraud is relatively common because "nobody is a victim" until the tax authority finds out, so firms in the chain may look the other way.
- Billions are generated each year that then need to be laundered.
- Factoring companies and banks can be part of the transaction chain, directly or indirectly. They should therefore apply due diligence to the actors they do business with.
- Large, well-known firms can also end up in the chain. It is not only small shell companies.

canonical_name: Fraud risk assessment blueprint — Fraud risk assessment workbook: layout — Introduction
description:
The workbook follows `_core/output-formats.md` and uses the same columns as the team's BWRA Excel template and the ABC workbook (AML analogy), so an integrated financial crime workbook can hold AML, ABC and fraud rows side by side.

Conventions:
- Every row has a unique ID.
- Every rating field has a drop-down list.
- Header rows are frozen.
- Data tables have no merged cells.

The **Detection coverage** sheet is restricted. Protect it, or deliver it as a separate file with limited distribution.

canonical_name: Fraud risk assessment blueprint — Fraud workshops, interviews and data request — 2.1 Context and exposure (team's contextual risk assessment)
description:
- What has changed in the last 12 months in products, services, channels, structure, strategy, market conditions, liabilities or customer relationships?
- How far does the current fraud management framework reach? Which products, channels and internal processes are not covered?
- Where in the organisation is fraud handled, and who owns the risk?
- How well can you detect internal fraud and infiltration today?

metadata.section: 2.1 Context and exposure (team's contextual risk assessment)

canonical_name: Fraud risk assessment blueprint — Fraud workshops, interviews and data request — 2.2 External fraud
description:
- Which fraud types cause the most losses, which cause the most attempts, and which are rising?
- How fast can a payment be stopped or recalled? Where is the last point at which a fraudulent payment can be intercepted?
- How are customer data and the customer risk assessment used to delay or stop suspicious payments?
- Which typologies have no detection rule or model? How was that decided?
- How do you balance detection sensitivity against blocking legitimate customers?
- How do fraud and AML cooperate on mule accounts?
- How are compensation decisions made for customers who were defrauded?

canonical_name: Fraud risk assessment blueprint — Fraud workshops, interviews and data request — 2.3 Internal fraud and infiltration
description:
- Who can change customer data, limits or payment details, and who reviews those changes?
- Who has privileged access to production systems? Are changes outside change management detected?
- Has the organisation seen cases of collusion, abuse of trusted positions or data leakage?
- Are staff approached or pressured by criminals, and how would they report it?
- How are the general ledger and suspense accounts reconciled, and who follows up exceptions?

canonical_name: Fraud risk assessment blueprint — Fraud workshops, interviews and data request — 2.4 Detection and models
description:
- Which rules and models exist? Are they documented, tuned, evaluated and validated, and how often?
- What are the alert volumes, the conversion rates and the backlog?
- What data is missing or of poor quality?

canonical_name: Gap analysis (gap log and gap report) blueprint — AMLR to national law: mapping guide (Sweden as worked example) — Introduction
description: This is the starting mapping between Regulation (EU) 2024/1624 (AMLR) and current Swedish rules, taken from the team's AMLR gap template. It is a **starting point, not a legal opinion**. Before use, check every reference against the current consolidated texts and the final AMLR text, and mark any uncertainty `[VERIFY REFERENCE]`. For other jurisdictions, replace the national column via `{{jurisdiction}}`.

canonical_name: Gap analysis (gap log and gap report) blueprint — AMLR to national law: mapping guide (Sweden as worked example) — 1. How to map
description:
1. **Backbone = the new instrument.** One row per paragraph, plus point level where a point carries its own obligation. Number rows Article.paragraph (e.g. 20.1).
2. **Find the national counterpart(s).** Enter the chapter and section (*kap.* and *§*, with *st.* or *p.* where useful) and quote the text in the next column. One AMLR paragraph often maps to several national provisions, and the reverse also happens.
3. **State the delta first** in "Extent of GAP":
   - *New* – no national equivalent.
   - *Amended* – an equivalent exists but the AMLR is stricter, more detailed or different in scope. Say how.
   - *Unchanged in substance* – the client's earlier compliance can be relied on if evidenced.
4. **Mark addressees.** Provisions addressed to Member States, the Commission, AMLA or supervisors are N/A for the obliged entity. Keep them visible for context.
5. **Flag Level 2.** Rows that announce RTS, ITS or guidelines are marked *Observe* until the measure is adopted. Many are due by 10 July 2026 or 10 July 2027 `[VERIFY REFERENCE: adoption status]`.
6. **National leftovers.** National provisions with no AMLR counterpart may be repealed, kept as options or moved. Do not assume they continue `[VERIFY REFERENCE: status of national adaptation]`.
7. **Client delta.** Only after steps 1–6, assess the client against the requirement (columns G–L of layout A).

- **Instructions**: purpose, reference framework and baseline date, colour legend, version log.

- **Summary**: a pivot, not typed by hand.

canonical_name: Gap analysis (gap log and gap report) blueprint — Gap log layouts (Excel) — A. AMLR mapped to national law (preferred standard)
description:
**Use for:** AMLR readiness; any change analysis where a new EU instrument replaces national rules.

**Sheets**
1. General provisions
2. Internal policies
3. CDD
4. BO transparency
5. Reporting obligations
6. Information sharing
7. Data protection and record retention
8. Measures to mitigate risks deriving from anonymous instruments
9. Final provisions

Then a **Scale** sheet (+ Instructions, Lists, Summary).

**Header block:** full title of the instrument in row 1. Row 2 holds the column headings. Row 3 holds a guidance line in brackets under each heading, which can be kept in the template and hidden in the deliverable.

| Column | Heading | Guidance row | Content rules |
|---|---|---|---|
| A | Article | — | Article.paragraph as in the instrument (e.g. 2.28, 9.2, 19.1). A heading row per article ("Article 20 Customer due diligence measures"). Section headings as separate rows ("Section 1 – General provisions"). |
| B | Description | — | Requirement text from the official source, one row per paragraph; separate rows for points that carry distinct obligations. |
| C | [National act title], e.g. "Lag (2017:630) om åtgärder mot penningtvätt och finansiering av terrorism" | [Current regulatory framework] | Reference to the corresponding provision(s), e.g. "2 kap. 8 och 13 §§ och 6 kap. 1 och 2 §§ PTL". Blank = no current equivalent (a new requirement). |
| D | (no heading) | — | Quoted text of the national provision. |
| E | Extent of GAP | [Analysis] | Starts with the regulatory delta (New / Amended / Unchanged + what changes), then the client's position. |
| F | Initial assessment | [Suggestion(s) on what to be done] | First view of what is needed; used in workshops; refined in column K. |
| G | Descriptions in internal regulations | [If applicable, description of information in internal regulations] | Document + section + short summary, or "Not mentioned". |

description:

**Sheets**
- AMLR: 1 General provisions … 9 Final provisions, then Annex I, Annex II, Annex III, Annex IV, Annex V, then Rullistor (Lists).
- RTS on CDD: Section 1 – Section 8 (following the draft RTS: identification and verification; purpose and intended nature; PEPs; simplified measures; enhanced measures; targeted financial sanctions; risk factors for e-money instruments; electronic identification means and qualified trust services), then ANNEX I (minimum attributes), then Rullistor.

| Column | Heading | Content |
|---|---|---|
| A | Article | As above |
| B | Description | Requirement text |
| C | Extent of GAP | Dropdown: N/A, Compliant, Minor, Limited, Major, Critical, Observe, ? |
| D | Initial assessment | Current state against the requirement, e.g. "Place of birth not collected today. New data point." |
| E | Action | Concrete action |
| F | Workstream | Project workstream (e.g. CDD, data, IT, governance) |
| G | Stakeholder(s) | Functions affected |
| H | Responsible | Accountable function |
| I | Links | Link to evidence, the policy draft or the backlog item |
| J | Status | Dropdown: Not started, Ongoing, Done |

**Annex I sheet (RTS):** Article 22(1) element | Minimum corresponding attributes | Extent of GAP | Initial assessment | Action | Workstream | Stakeholder | Responsible.

canonical_name: Gap analysis (gap log and gap report) blueprint — Gap log layouts (Excel) — C. National law and supervisory regulations (Swedish baseline template)
description:
**Use for:** baseline compliance under current national rules.

**Sheets**
- *Bedömningskriterier* (assessment criteria): GAP = JA / NEJ; Gradering = Kritiska brister, Omfattande brister, Betydande brister, Mindre brister, Inga brister.
- PTL.
- FFFS 2017:11, or the county administrative board's regulations for entities it supervises `[VERIFY REFERENCE]`.

The older templates' paragraph overview sheet is marked by the team as "consider removing". Replace it with the calculated Summary.

| Column (Swedish heading) | English | Content |
|---|---|---|
| Kapitel och paragraf | Chapter and section | e.g. "2 kap.", "8 § 1 st.", one row per *stycke* (subsection) |
| Innehåll | Content | Text of the provision |
| GAP (Ja/Nej) | GAP (Yes/No) | Ja / Nej / Ej tillämpligt |
| Beskrivning av GAP | Description of gap | The gap description |
| Gradering av GAP | Gap rating | The 5-level scale |
| Kommentar | Comment | Clarifications, meeting outcomes |
| Ev hänvisning till interna styrdokument | Reference to internal governing documents | Document + section |

A bilingual variant (for an internationally staffed client with a Swedish licence) groups rows by **Principal area** (e.g. A.1 Governance) and has these columns: PTL (ENG) | PTL (SWE) | FFFS 2017:11 (ENG) | FFFS 2017:11 (SWE). The FFFS provision is placed on the same row as the PTL provision it implements. Label the English texts as unofficial translations.

canonical_name: Gap analysis (gap log and gap report) blueprint — Gap log layouts (Excel) — G. Document evidence matrix
description:
**Use for:** framework-component scans, such as a sanctions compliance programme. Columns are the framework's elements, grouped by component (e.g. management commitment, risk assessment, internal controls, testing and auditing, training). Rows are the client's documents: Policy, Directive/Instruction, Risk assessment.

| Symbol | English | Swedish |
|---|---|---|
| + | Record | *Dokumentation finns* |
| X | No record | *Ingen dokumentation* |
| NO DATA | Records not obtained | *Dokumentation inte mottagen* |

This distinguishes missing documents from documents not provided. Follow it with the substantive assessment in layout A, C or E.

canonical_name: Gap analysis (gap log and gap report) blueprint — Gap templates for other frameworks — 2. Sanctions compliance programme: OFAC framework components
description:
The framework is OFAC's Framework for Compliance Commitments `[VERIFY REFERENCE]`. Use layout G (document evidence matrix) first, then a substantive assessment.

| Component | Elements (columns) |
|---|---|
| Management commitment | Sanctions compliance programme in place; compliance given authority and autonomy to apply policies and procedures; adequate resources (staff, IT, other); culture of compliance promoted; seriousness of apparent violations recognised |
| Risk assessment | Sanctions risk assessment; method to identify, analyse and address the specific risks identified |
| Internal controls | Internal controls that reflect the risk assessment and risk profile; policies and procedures maintained; documentation of guidance; immediate action when a weakness in internal controls is identified; policies and procedures communicated to relevant staff; staff designated to embed them in daily operations |
| Testing and auditing | Testing or audit function accountable to senior management; procedures appropriate to the level and complexity of the programme; immediate and effective action on negative results |
| Training | `[VERIFY REFERENCE: training elements]` |

Rows: Policy | Directive/Instruction | Risk assessment. Values: + Record / X No record / NO DATA Records not obtained.

For EU-based clients, add EU and UN sanctions regimes and national implementing rules via `{{jurisdiction}}`, and consider the `sanctions-risk-assessment` blueprint.

Use layout F. Sections as structured in the team template (guidelines under Article 13(1) of Directive (EU) 2015/849) `[VERIFY REFERENCE: EBA/GL number and whether superseded under the AMLR]`:

- 4.1 Internal policies and procedures
  - 4.1.1 Policies and procedures for remote onboarding
  - 4.1.2 Governance (compliance officer role, management body approval)
  - 4.1.3 Pre-implementation assessment of the solution
  - 4.1.4 Ongoing monitoring of the solution
- 4.2 Acquisition of information
  - 4.2.1 Identifying the customer
  - 4.2.2 Natural persons
  - 4.2.3 Legal entities
  - 4.2.4 Nature and purpose of the business relationship
- 4.3 Document authenticity and integrity
- 4.4 Matching the customer's identity as part of verification (biometrics, liveness, attended and unattended solutions)
- 4.5 Reliance on third parties and outsourcing (4.5.1 reliance; 4.5.2 outsourcing of CDD)
- 4.6 ICT and security risk management
- 4.7 Use of trust services and national electronic identification processes

Under the AMLR, the corresponding Level 2 content sits in the RTS on CDD (non-face-to-face verification; electronic identification means). Map both if the client is preparing for the AMLR.
