canonical_name: Training and presentations blueprint — Module: International sanctions — Learning objectives
description:
1. Explain what a sanction is, who adopts it and how it applies to the client.
2. Explain the difference between AML (obligations, risk-based) and sanctions (prohibitions, strict liability).
3. Handle a screening hit: true or false match, freeze, report.
4. Apply ownership and control rules to a corporate structure.
5. Recognise circumvention patterns.
6. (Management) Explain the EBA guidelines' requirements and the AMLR integration.

canonical_name: Training and presentations blueprint — Module: International sanctions — Block 01 – Theoretical framework (about 45 min)
description:
1. **What is a "sanction"?** – "non-armed coercive measures adopted by a state or organisation to put pressure on and ultimately induce a change in behaviour". There is always a political objective; a sanction is never an end in itself; "the means of a sanction are not always the same as its ends".
2. **Ambiguity of terminology** – international, economic, financial, administrative sanctions, restrictive measures.
3. **Historical development** – early US wartime trade powers (1917); UN Charter mandate for binding Security Council sanctions (1945); US emergency economic powers as basis for OFAC programmes (1977); EU's own restrictive measures under the Common Foreign and Security Policy (Article 29 TEU, Article 215 TFEU); the 2014 Russia/Ukraine regulations (EU 269/2014 and 833/2014); 2022 onwards: record number of EU packages.
4. **Actors** – UN (binding on all members); EU (Council, unanimity; the primary regime for EU institutions); OFAC (global reach through the US dollar); UK; others, including counter-sanctions and anti-foreign-sanctions laws.
5. **Fundamentals of EU sanctions** – legal basis and unanimity (affects speed and scope); targets: individuals, entities, sectors, states; measures: asset freezes, travel bans, arms embargoes, trade and financial restrictions; more than 30 regimes `[DATA NEEDED: current number]`.
6. **Applicability** – targeted (persons and entities; asset freezes) vs sectoral (sectors, goods, services, capital); ownership and control: a listed person's ownership or control of a company extends the measures to it, including control without formal ownership (influence, contracts, proxies).

canonical_name: Training and presentations blueprint — Module: International sanctions — Block 01 – Theoretical framework (about 45 min)
description:
7. **Sanctions and AML – what is the difference?** – AML = obligations (risk assessment, CDD), risk-based thresholds, responsibility for compliance not occurrence, targets identified through risk factors. Sanctions = prohibitions, strict liability for compliance, real-time implementation, no value thresholds, targets named or clearly defined. Examples: freeze of listed persons' assets (EU 269/2014, Article 2(1)); reporting of deposits above EUR 100,000 by certain Russian nationals and entities (EU 833/2014) `[VERIFY REFERENCE: article]`.
8. **Closing the compliance gap** – no clear EU-level compliance requirements led to uneven implementation, breaches and de-risking; guidelines and AMLR integration address this.
9. **The two EBA guidelines on restrictive measures (EBA/GL/2024/14 and EBA/GL/2024/15)** `[VERIFY REFERENCE: confirm which number applies to which]` – the general guideline (all financial institutions in scope): governance (board, CEO, a senior staff member responsible; placement flexible, conflicts of interest to be avoided), risk assessment (identify applicable regimes, assess likelihood of breach or circumvention, consider customers, geographies, products and channels, document and update, local assessments in subsidiaries), controls, training (regular and role-specific). The guideline for payment and crypto-asset service providers: screening, match analysis and decisions, circumvention detection, freezing and reporting, systems and governance; applied in line with the general guideline.
10. **Implementation and expected outcome** – proportionality, harmonisation, fewer breaches, fewer wrongful freezes; application date and the transfer of mandates to AMLA `[VERIFY REFERENCE: dates]`.

canonical_name: Training and presentations blueprint — Module: International sanctions — Block 01 – Theoretical framework (about 45 min)
description:
11. **Status in relation to AMLR and AMLA** – the AMLR integrates sanctions-evasion risk into the AML framework from 2027 and prevails in case of conflict; current guidelines are general, so implementation work is not wasted.
12. **Where to start?** – risk assessment (decides which controls and priorities); alignment with AML (documentation, maintenance, integration); training (general and role-specific, as for AML); screening and list management as part of model risk management (document gaps; dynamic lists make input data critical).
13. **Conclusion** – sanctions ≠ AML: sanctions drive behaviour, AML stops illicit funds; key actors; why guidelines; core requirements; timeline.

canonical_name: Training and presentations blueprint — Module: International sanctions — Block 02 – Interactive discussion (about 45 min)
description:
1. **Poll** on the participants' current set-up and challenges.
2. **Sanction approaches** – reactive, active, proactive across customers, products, onboarding, counterparties, transactions, contracts, holdings, trading, customer stock; an "active look-back" database to learn from.
3. **Practical screening** – customers (names, aliases, spellings, date of birth, nationality, address, relationships; legal names and trading names, registration number, sector, jurisdiction, ownership); delta vs full screening; transactions (payment message standards); "things" (goods: tariff codes, dual-use and export control lists; securities: identifiers, issuer, trading restrictions; vessels and aircraft: IMO number, flag state, ownership, AIS tracking for ship-to-ship transfers).
4. **Speed of business** – slow flows (batch screening, time to investigate and contact the customer) vs fast flows (instant payments, settlement, onboarding: "no time to stop", rules, tuning and testing, alerts needing instant attention).
5. **Set-up of screening** – customer experience and potential avoidance; flows exempted as low risk or too fast; screening while money is in transit.
6. **Risk-based approach to sanctions** – type of customer, transaction type, severity, pattern, information and context, lists and entities.
7. **Deployment and change management** – test, test, test with FCP, business and tech; an active look-back database; run in shadow mode in production where possible.

canonical_name: Training and presentations blueprint — Module: International sanctions — Bank workshop extensions (half day)
description:
- **Hits – what do we do?** EU list: freeze (no interest credited etc.), report to the supervisor, then wait for decisions on exemptions; missed reporting: report afterwards and consider whether it is a significant event. US lists: blocking and reject reports within the US deadline `[VERIFY REFERENCE]`; voluntary self-disclosure; seek US legal advice.
- **Investigation and escalation flow** – screening at onboarding and ongoing → suspected hit → investigation → suspicion dismissed (documented in the customer file, any freeze lifted) or not dismissed (funds frozen, report to the supervisor, possibly to the FIU; for US exposure, reporting to US authorities).
- **True vs false match** (case C-16) and **weak aliases**; cultural and linguistic knowledge of names; whitelisting with caution.
- **Fuzzy matching** – phonetic similarity, transliteration, nicknames, missing spaces and hyphens, titles, truncated, missing or reordered name parts, initials, names split across fields, same name in several languages.
- **Sanctions risk assessment** – data collection largely the same as for ML/TF; overall assessment along the OFAC framework or as extra fields in the ML/TF assessment; specific risks (circumvention) treated like typologies; controls assessed for design and effectiveness at the same time as the ML/TF assessment.
- **Circumvention** – straw men (relatives, drivers, former spouses, household staff who suddenly own significant companies); aliases, name changes, bought passports; dual citizenship and "golden passports"; false flags and labels; re-export through neighbouring countries and hubs; complex structures and hidden beneficial owners.

canonical_name: Training and presentations blueprint — Module: International sanctions — Bank workshop extensions (half day)
description:
- **Sanctions in KYC and monitoring** – who is the customer (and who else is screened: suppliers, employees, payees, correspondent banks); risk classification must include sanctions risk factors; purpose and nature can reveal circumvention; "Do funds come from or go to a sanctioned party? Is this a sanctions straw man?"
- **US compliance framework** – management commitment, risk assessment, internal controls, testing and auditing, training.
- **How do others do it?** – sanctions in the financial crime policy or a separate policy; risk appetite; risk assessment; a unit in the FCP function plus compliance control; customer and payment screening with validated fuzzy logic; deeper investigations.
- **Maturity grid** – *Focused (high exposure) / Balanced (normal exposure) / Insufficient (risk-taking)* for management commitment, sanctions risk assessment, internal controls, customer screening, beneficial ownership and EDD, payment screening, goods and securities, reporting, testing and auditing, and training (focused: general training for all staff, specialised training and certifications; balanced: separate sanctions training for board, compliance, AML and relevant customer-facing staff; insufficient: sanctions mentioned briefly in AML training).

canonical_name: Training and presentations blueprint — Module: International sanctions — Open-course variant (five facts)
description: Five facts: purpose; types (broad or targeted, travel, listing, trade, financial); regimes (UN, EU, US, UK); five heavily sanctioned countries `[DATA NEEDED: current]`; risk-based vs absolute ("so how do we do it in practice?"). Then: national sanctions system and competent authorities; US nexus; ownership rules with situations 1–5 (case C-12); cases C-13 to C-15; shadow designations; handling of a true hit and the content of the freeze report (name, legal basis with article and annex, date, amount or value, specification of what is frozen); components of an effective programme (dedicated officer, resources, policy and processes, risk assessment, committee for high-risk customers, due diligence beyond the customer); lessons learned (under-estimated resources, misunderstanding US reach, poorly tuned screening, broken tools, ignored third-party risk, insufficient KYC, no process for shadow designations, weak independent review); useful public websites.

canonical_name: Training and presentations blueprint — Quiz and knowledge-check bank — Foundations (module-aml-ctf-foundations)
description:
| Q-ID | Lvl | Type | Question or statement | Answer | Rationale |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Q-FND-01 | A | TF | To report to the FIU, you need proof that money laundering has taken place. | False | Reasonable grounds to suspect are enough; the threshold for suspicion is low. The FIU puts together information from many sources. |
| Q-FND-02 | A | MC | The three stages of money laundering are: A) placement, layering, integration B) collection, storage, use C) identification, verification, monitoring | A | B describes terrorist financing (collection, storage, movement, use); C describes KYC steps. |
| Q-FND-03 | A | TF | Terrorist financing always involves criminal proceeds. | False | Funds can come from legitimate sources such as donations, salaries or loans; the concern is where the money goes. |
| Q-FND-04 | B | MC | What forms the basis of all the entity's measures against ML/TF? A) The customer risk classification B) The business-wide risk assessment C) The transaction monitoring system | B | The BWRA decides the routines, the risk classification, the monitoring and the training. |
| Q-FND-05 | A | TF | The AML rules specify exactly which controls each firm must have. | False | The rules are risk-based: the firm decides and must be able to justify its measures. |
| Q-FND-06 | D | TF | Board members are also bound by the prohibition on disclosing that a report has been made. | True | The prohibition covers the entity, its board members and employees (SE). |
| Q-FND-07 | B | TF | The quality of transaction monitoring can never be higher than the quality of KYC. | True | Monitoring looks for deviations from expected behaviour; KYC defines what is expected. |

canonical_name: Training and presentations blueprint — Quiz and knowledge-check bank — Risk assessment and customer risk classification (module-risk-assessment-and-crc)
description:
| Q-ID | Lvl | Type | Question or statement | Answer | Rationale |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Q-RA-01 | B | MC | Which four risk categories must the BWRA at least cover? A) Products and services, customers, distribution channels, geography B) Credit, market, liquidity, operational C) Fraud, sanctions, ABC, tax | A | These are the risk factor categories in the AML rules and the EBA risk factor guidelines. |
| Q-RA-02 | B | TF | Residual risk is the risk that remains when controls have been applied to the inherent risk. | True | Inherent risk, then controls, then residual risk – kept apart and shown step by step. |
| Q-RA-03 | C | TF | Weighting of risk factors may be designed so that customers are never classified as high risk. | False | The EBA risk factor guidelines say weighting must not lead to high risk never being applied, and financial considerations must not drive it. |
| Q-RA-04 | B | TF | The BWRA only needs to cover money laundering; terrorist financing is handled by sanctions screening. | False | Both ML and TF risk must be assessed, and the supervisor expects them to be distinguished. |
| Q-RA-05 | C | SC | In a scoring model, a high-risk country gives 40 points and "high risk" starts at 40 points. What is the problem? | One factor alone decides the class | Single-value models let one factor dominate; a multi-factor or risk-weighted model spreads risk across factors. |
| Q-RA-06 | B | TF | A customer's risk class should be reassessed when the customer starts using a new product. | True | Risk classification is dynamic: new products, behaviour, geography or ownership changes trigger reassessment. |
| Q-RA-07 | C | TF | An AML risk assessment where all residual risks end up "Normal" is usually a sign of a mature process. | False | It usually signals vague risk descriptions, undocumented controls or no control testing; supervisors challenge it. |

canonical_name: Training and presentations blueprint — Quiz and knowledge-check bank — KYC, beneficial ownership and PEP (module-kyc-cdd-pep)
description:
| Q-ID | Lvl | Type | Question or statement | Answer | Rationale |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Q-KYC-01 | B | TF | Information from the customer's own website can be used to verify the customer's identity. | False | It can be used to identify (obtain information) but generally not to verify. The credibility of the source is decisive. |
| Q-KYC-02 | A | MC | "Buying a TV on credit" and "monthly instalments of SEK 400 over 12 months" describe: A) purpose and nature B) nature and purpose C) source of funds and source of wealth | A | Purpose is the *why*, nature is the *how* (volumes, flows). |
| Q-KYC-03 | B | TF | A PEP's sibling is a family member under the Swedish definition. (SE) | False | Family members are spouse, registered partner, cohabitee, children and their spouses, partners or cohabitees, and parents. Siblings are not included. |
| Q-KYC-04 | B | TF | Regional and municipal politicians are PEPs under the Swedish definition. (SE) | False | Only the national and international level is covered; a case-by-case assessment is still needed for unclear functions. |
| Q-KYC-05 | B | TF | In Sweden, enhanced PEP measures apply for 18 months after the person leaves the function, and after that only if the risk is assessed as high. (SE) | True | Money Laundering Act, chapter 3, section 20 (SE). The EU minimum is shorter `[VERIFY REFERENCE]`. |
| Q-KYC-06 | B | TF | The list of important public functions in the law is exhaustive. | False | It is exemplifying ("such as"); assess each case, apply caution and document the reasoning in unclear cases. |
| Q-KYC-07 | B | MC | If the customer's beneficial owner is a PEP, which applies? A) Simplified measures B) Source of funds, enhanced monitoring and approval by an authorised decision-maker C) Automatic exit | B | These enhanced measures always apply for PEPs and their family members and known close associates. |

canonical_name: Training and presentations blueprint — Quiz and knowledge-check bank — KYC, beneficial ownership and PEP (module-kyc-cdd-pep)
description:
| Q-ID | Lvl | Type | Question or statement | Answer | Rationale |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Q-KYC-08 | B | TF | If no natural person can be identified as beneficial owner, the customer can never be accepted. | False | After exhausting the means, and if there is no suspicion, an alternative beneficial owner (CEO, chair or equivalent) is designated and the steps documented. |
| Q-KYC-09 | A | TF | Low-risk customers do not need any periodic review. | False | Reviews are still required, less often and less intensive (typically every 3–5 years, per the client's policy). |
| Q-KYC-10 | B | SC | Screening of a company gives no hits and the customer declares no PEPs. Is that enough when a foreign foundation sits in the ownership chain? | No | Identify and screen the natural persons behind the foundation; a self-declaration does not replace beneficial-owner investigation. |

canonical_name: Training and presentations blueprint — Quiz and knowledge-check bank — Monitoring, investigation and reporting (module-monitoring-and-reporting)
description:
| Q-ID | Lvl | Type | Question or statement | Answer | Rationale |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Q-TM-01 | A | TF | The purpose of transaction monitoring is to prove a crime. | False | It detects activity that does not match what we know about the customer; deviation leads to attention, not to proof. |
| Q-TM-02 | B | TF | The reporting obligation ends when the business relationship is terminated. | False | It continues after termination and also covers refused transactions and relationships. |
| Q-TM-03 | B | TF | You should always contact the customer before reporting. | False | In obvious cases of suspicion the customer is not contacted; report without delay. |
| Q-TM-04 | B | TF | An internal investigation should be as thorough as a police investigation. | False | It only assesses whether there is reason to suspect ML/TF. |
| Q-TM-05 | A | MC | Which three concepts describe a change in a customer's behaviour? A) Volume, frequency, pattern B) Age, income, address C) Product, channel, geography | A | Pattern combines volume and frequency; peer comparison and typology matching add depth. |
| Q-TM-06 | B | TF | If a customer has always behaved in a certain way, that behaviour is by definition normal. | False | Past behaviour is not proof of legitimacy; what is deviant for one customer may be normal for another. |
| Q-TM-07 | B | MC | Which of these must the documentation of a suspicious case contain? A) Who reviewed, reason for suspicion, actions and rationale, analysis, decisions and reasoning, timing B) Only the final decision C) The customer's consent | A | So that the assessment can be followed and defended afterwards. |
| Q-TM-08 | A | TF | A report to the FIU is the same as a criminal complaint to the police. | False | It is an intelligence report; the FIU decides on further action. |

canonical_name: Training and presentations blueprint — Quiz and knowledge-check bank — Monitoring, investigation and reporting (module-monitoring-and-reporting)
description:
| Q-ID | Lvl | Type | Question or statement | Answer | Rationale |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Q-TM-09 | A | TF | KYC documentation and records must be kept for five years after the business relationship has ended. | True | Money Laundering Act, chapter 5, section 3 (SE); the EU baseline is also five years. |
| Q-TM-10 | B | SC | A third party repays a customer's whole credit. Name three things you check. | e.g. who the payer is and the relationship; source of the payer's funds; purpose and age of the loan | Third-party repayment is a known placement method in credit products. |

canonical_name: Training and presentations blueprint — Quiz and knowledge-check bank — Sanctions (module-sanctions)
description:
| Q-ID | Lvl | Type | Question or statement | Answer | Rationale |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Q-SAN-01 | B | TF | Sanctions compliance, like AML, is based on value thresholds. | False | AML is risk-based with risk-based thresholds; sanctions are prohibitions with strict liability and no value thresholds. How deep screening goes is still a risk-based choice. |
| Q-SAN-02 | A | TF | AML is about obligations; sanctions are about prohibitions. | True | A useful one-liner for the difference. |
| Q-SAN-03 | B | TF | Sweden has its own national sanctions lists. (SE) | False | Sweden applies EU sanctions (including UN sanctions adopted by the EU); breaches are criminal under national law. `[VERIFY REFERENCE: current status of any national sanctions regime]` |
| Q-SAN-04 | B | MC | A customer is confirmed as listed under EU sanctions. What do you do? A) Close the account and pay out the balance B) Freeze the funds and report to the supervisor C) Wait for the customer to contact you | B | Freeze without delay; in Sweden report to Finansinspektionen; consider an FIU report. Do not pay out. |
| Q-SAN-05 | B | TF | US sanctions can apply to a Swedish bank without any US branch. | True | A US nexus arises through USD payments, US correspondent banks, US persons or US-origin goods and technology. |
| Q-SAN-06 | C | TF | Under OFAC rules, a company owned 25% each by two listed persons is blocked. | True | Ownership by blocked persons is aggregated: 50% or more in aggregate. |
| Q-SAN-07 | B | TF | The purpose of investigating a screening hit is to detect suspicious behaviour. | False | The purpose is to establish whether the hit is the same person or entity; circumvention investigations are a separate question. |

canonical_name: Training and presentations blueprint — Quiz and knowledge-check bank — Sanctions (module-sanctions)
description:
| Q-ID | Lvl | Type | Question or statement | Answer | Rationale |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Q-SAN-08 | C | TF | Under the AMLR, the risk of non-implementation and evasion of targeted financial sanctions is part of the business-wide risk assessment. | True | `[VERIFY REFERENCE: AMLR article on the business-wide risk assessment]` |

canonical_name: Training and presentations blueprint — Quiz and knowledge-check bank — ABC (module-abc)
description:
| Q-ID | Lvl | Type | Question or statement | Answer | Rationale |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Q-ABC-01 | A | TF | There are specific amount limits for what counts as a bribe. | False | Whether a benefit is improper is assessed case by case: purpose, link to duties, intent and general practice. |
| Q-ABC-02 | A | TF | An offer of a bribe that is not accepted cannot be prosecuted. | False | Giving a bribe includes offering or promising an improper benefit (SE). |
| Q-ABC-03 | C | TF | Sweden has a general corporate offence of "failure to prevent bribery" like the UK Bribery Act. | False | Sweden has negligent financing of bribery (*vårdslös finansiering av mutbrott*) and corporate fines `[VERIFY REFERENCE]`. |
| Q-ABC-04 | A | TF | Bribery is a predicate offence to money laundering. | True | Bribes are criminal proceeds that need to be laundered. |
| Q-ABC-05 | B | MC | Which is NOT an ABC control? A) Separation of duties B) Two signatures on payment approvals C) Letting the person who introduced an intermediary approve its invoices | C | That combination removes the separation of duties. |

canonical_name: Training and presentations blueprint — Quiz and knowledge-check bank — Fraud (module-fraud)
description:
| Q-ID | Lvl | Type | Question or statement | Answer | Rationale |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Q-FR-01 | B | TF | In a VAT carousel, every company in the chain must know about the fraud. | False | Others in the chain can be unaware; if they should have known, they risk losing VAT deductions and liability. |
| Q-FR-02 | B | MC | Which goods are typical in intra-community VAT fraud? A) Fresh food B) Mobile phones, computer chips, emission allowances C) Real estate | B | High value, small volume, easy to move – often only ownership changes. |
| Q-FR-03 | A | TF | Tax crime can be a predicate offence to money laundering. | True | Tax crimes generate large proceeds that need laundering. |

canonical_name: Training and presentations blueprint — Quiz and knowledge-check bank — Model risk management (module-model-risk-management)
description:
| Q-ID | Lvl | Type | Question or statement | Answer | Rationale |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Q-MRM-01 | C | TF | A process must use statistical methods to count as a model. | False | The Swedish supervisor's definition covers procedures that automate or standardise assessments under the AML Act. |
| Q-MRM-02 | C | TF | If the institution has not classified a process as a model, the supervisor will not either. | False | Model identification is part of model risk management; a missed model is not an excuse. |
| Q-MRM-03 | C | MC | When must a model be validated? A) Only when the supervisor asks B) Before use, after significant changes, and periodically based on model risk C) Once every five years | B | Initial validation before production; limited-scope validation before significant changes; risk-based periodic validation. |
| Q-MRM-04 | C | MC | Model risk is commonly assessed by combining: A) criticality and quality B) cost and benefit C) age and size | A | Criticality decides how important good quality is; quality changes more often. |
| Q-MRM-05 | C | TF | A daily update of sanctions lists is a significant model change. | False | List updates are routine; changes to thresholds or matching logic may be significant. |

canonical_name: Training and presentations blueprint — Quiz and knowledge-check bank — Governance and roles (module-governance-and-roles)
description:
| Q-ID | Lvl | Type | Question or statement | Answer | Rationale |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Q-GOV-01 | C | TF | The special appointed executive (SAE) is an additional control function. | False | The SAE is a member of management who makes sure measures are implemented; the CFA is the independent control function. |
| Q-GOV-02 | C | TF | A CFA must always be appointed; an SAE when justified by the size and nature of the business. (SE) | True | FFFS 2017:11 and the AML Act (SE) `[VERIFY REFERENCE]`. |
| Q-GOV-03 | D | MC | Which is a useful risk indicator for board reporting? A) Number of slides in the training B) Share of staff who have completed AML/CTF training C) Number of meetings held | B | Together with high-risk customers, FIU reports, reviewed alerts and overdue findings. |
| Q-GOV-04 | D | TF | Risk appetite only needs to be set at strategic level. | False | It works at strategic (business model, geography), tactical (organisation, processes) and operational (onboarding, alert escalation) level. |

canonical_name: Training and presentations blueprint — Quiz and knowledge-check bank — FATCA and CRS (module-other-topics)
description:
| Q-ID | Lvl | Type | Question or statement | Answer | Rationale |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Q-TAX-01 | B | TF | FATCA is an OECD standard applied in over 100 jurisdictions. | False | FATCA is US legislation; CRS is the OECD standard. |
| Q-TAX-02 | B | TF | A person tax resident only in Sweden but a Norwegian citizen is reportable under CRS because of the citizenship. | False | CRS is based on tax residence, not citizenship. |
| Q-TAX-03 | B | TF | A person tax resident in Sweden who is a US citizen is reportable under FATCA. | True | FATCA covers US persons, including citizens, subject to the applicable thresholds and exceptions. |
| Q-TAX-04 | B | TF | A FATCA/CRS self-certification replaces KYC. | False | It complements KYC; KYC information is also reviewed for indicia. |

canonical_name: Training and presentations blueprint — Quiz and knowledge-check bank — AMLR outlook (module-regulatory-outlook)
description:
| Q-ID | Lvl | Type | Question or statement | Answer | Rationale |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Q-AMLR-01 | B | TF | The AMLR is a directive that each member state transposes into national law. | False | It is a regulation, directly applicable; AMLD6 is the directive that member states transpose. |
| Q-AMLR-02 | B | MC | The AMLR generally applies from: A) 1 January 2026 B) 10 July 2027 C) 1 July 2030 | B | Check for any provisions with different dates `[VERIFY REFERENCE]`. |

canonical_name: Training and presentations blueprint — Training records and evaluation
description: Reference catalogue `references/training-records-and-evaluation.md` of the FCP blueprint `training-and-presentations` (skill fcp-bp-training-and-presentations). Sections: Introduction; 1. What the evidence pack must show; 2. Training plan and target-group matrix (workbook); 3. Attendance and results register; 4. Evaluation form; 5. Question and answer log; 6. KPIs and KRIs; 7. Summary note after the training (1–2 pages); 8. Retention

canonical_name: Training and presentations blueprint — Training records and evaluation — Introduction
description:
How to document completed training so that the client can show its supervisor that training is risk-based, role-specific, ongoing and actually delivered. This is the "training log" (*utbildningslogg*) part of the deliverable.

Basis: the obligation to train (SKILL.md section 4) implies the ability to evidence it. The team's material shows training as an item in the CFA's risk-based annual plan, as a KRI reported to the board ("number who have completed the training on measures against ML/TF"), and, for ABC under ISO 37001, as "evidence of regular training catering to the needs of general staff and key functions". The register and evaluation layouts below are the team's standard proposal; where the client has its own learning system or HR template, use that and map the fields.

canonical_name: Training and presentations blueprint — Training records and evaluation — 1. What the evidence pack must show
description:
| Question a supervisor or auditor asks | Evidence |
|---|---|
| Is training based on the risks in the BWRA? | Design brief or summary note linking modules to BWRA risks; deck version |
| Is it adapted to roles? | Target-group matrix: role × module × depth × frequency |
| Was it delivered, and to whom? | Attendance register per session; e-learning completion export |
| Did participants understand it? | Knowledge-check results; pass rate; retakes |
| Is it ongoing and up to date? | Training plan by year; version history of the material; regulatory status date on the deck |
| Are new staff and the board covered? | Onboarding completion within the agreed period; board training minuted |
| Are gaps followed up? | Overdue list, reminders, escalation; KRI reporting to management and board |

metadata.section: 1. What the evidence pack must show

canonical_name: Training and presentations blueprint — Training records and evaluation — 2. Training plan and target-group matrix (workbook)
description:
Follow `_core/output-formats.md` section 3. Sheets:

1. **Instructions** – purpose, colour legend, version log.
2. **Target groups**

| Column | Content |
|---|---|
| TG-ID | e.g. TG-01 |
| Target group | e.g. Customer service, Credit, Payments, AML function, Management, Board, Agents/outsourced staff |
| Example roles | |
| Headcount | `[DATA NEEDED]` |
| Depth level | A / B / C / D (SKILL.md 7.1) |
| Key BWRA risks for this group | From the BWRA |

3. **Modules**

| Column | Content |
|---|---|
| M-ID | e.g. M-KYC-01 |
| Module | Name from the module library |
| Format | Classroom / digital / e-learning |
| Duration (min) | |
| Version and date | e.g. v2.1, 2026-09-01 |
| Regulatory status as of | Date |
| Owner | Function (e.g. CFA) |

4. **Matrix** – TG-ID × M-ID with values *Mandatory / Recommended / –*, plus **Frequency** (at onboarding, annually, on change) and **Deadline** (e.g. within a set number of weeks of starting `[TO CONFIRM]`).
5. **Plan** – per quarter: session, module, target group, date, trainer, status (*Planned / Held / Cancelled*). Align with the CFA's annual plan, where annual staff training and a tailored management or board training are separate items.
6. **Register** – see section 3.
7. **KPIs** – see section 6.

canonical_name: Training and presentations blueprint — Training records and evaluation — 3. Attendance and results register
description:
One row per participant per session. Use an employee ID or role where the client prefers to minimise personal data; names are held in the client's system, not in our deliverable.

| Column | Content |
|---|---|
| Session ID | e.g. S-2026-07 |
| Date | ISO date |
| Module / M-ID | |
| Material version | Deck version used |
| Format | Classroom / digital / e-learning |
| Trainer | Role or firm |
| Participant ID | Employee ID (or name in the client's own system) |
| Role / target group | TG-ID |
| Attended | Yes / No / Partly |
| Duration (min) | |
| Knowledge check score | % |
| Passed | Yes / No |
| Retake date | |
| Comment | e.g. left early, follow-up needed |

Board training: record in the board minutes (date, topic, presenters, material attached) and in the register.

canonical_name: Training and presentations blueprint — Training records and evaluation — 4. Evaluation form
description:
Scale 1–5 (1 = not at all, 5 = fully):

1. The training was relevant to my role.
2. The content was clear.
3. The examples and exercises were useful.
4. The pace and length were right.
5. I know what to do if I suspect money laundering, terrorist financing, a sanctions breach or bribery. [adapt to topic]

Open questions:
- What will you do differently after this training?
- What was missing or unclear?
- Other comments.

Summarise as average per question, response rate, and the three most common comments.

canonical_name: Training and presentations blueprint — Training records and evaluation — 5. Question and answer log
description:
| # | Session | Question | Asked by (role) | Answer | Source / reference | Answered by | Date answered |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|

Questions not answered in the session are answered in writing after it; the log goes into the summary note.

canonical_name: Training and presentations blueprint — Training records and evaluation — 6. KPIs and KRIs
description:
| Indicator | Definition | Typical use |
|---|---|---|
| Completion rate | Trained ÷ target group, per period and target group | KRI to management and board |
| Overdue | Number not trained by the deadline | Follow-up and escalation |
| New joiners on time | Share of new staff trained within the onboarding deadline | KRI |
| Average score / pass rate | Mean knowledge-check score; share passing at first attempt | Quality of training and understanding |
| Evaluation | Average relevance score | Improve the material |
| Board and management | Date of last board training; topics | Governance reporting |

Thresholds for KRIs (e.g. completion below a set percentage triggers escalation) are set in the client's risk appetite `[TO CONFIRM]`.

canonical_name: Training and presentations blueprint — Training records and evaluation — 7. Summary note after the training (1–2 pages)
description:
| Section | Content |
|---|---|
| 1 Training held | Date, format, topic, target group, presenters, material version, regulatory status date |
| 2 Link to the BWRA | Which risks the training addressed and why |
| 3 Participation and results | Attended vs invited; knowledge-check results; evaluation summary |
| 4 Observations | What the discussion showed: recurring questions, uncertainty about the internal route, gaps in understanding, input to the BWRA or to internal rules |
| 5 Recommendations | Follow-up training, topics for next year, changes to procedures or instructions, need for role-specific sessions |
| 6 Annex | Q&A log, attendance export, slides |

Write the note so the CFA can attach it to the periodic report to management and board. Observations about weaknesses are factual and constructive; they are reported, not softened.

metadata.section: 7. Summary note after the training (1–2 pages)

canonical_name: Training and presentations blueprint — Training records and evaluation — 8. Retention
description: Keep the deck version, attendance, results and evaluation for as long as the client's retention policy requires `[TO CONFIRM: client's retention period]`, and at least long enough to cover the supervisor's look-back in an inspection. Personal data in registers follows the client's data protection rules.
